utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. After this short training in experience this morning, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. I see that all the computers, I hope, are functioning properly. Mr. Ierace, did I see that you wanted to raise --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And a few matters that perhaps I could raise in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then turn in to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Then Madam Usher, could you please escort the Witness DP35 into the courtroom. The public gallery is empty, as far as I can see. Facial distortion and pseudonym are the applicable protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be happy to do so. And I'd like to make it clear that since we were not able to join copies because in our chamber things were not working properly. But never mind. I should like to say now good morning to the Chamber and to go back to what we addressed yesterday, the subject that we broached yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that we were talking about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I remind you, Mr. DP35, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony in this court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we remember that we talked about the area of Dobrinja, and you pointed at two Serb positions. And in response to Judge Nieto-Navia, you said it was very difficult to know from where shots came under wartime conditions. This is a summary of what you said yesterday. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, my question is as follows: Since you said that it was difficult to know where and how the shots were fired, can you tell us, when we talk about the military confrontation, that is, the fire, what happened between the positions that you described yesterday and the Serb positions to the south-south-west of the airport, and the adversary positions facing them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Dobrinja I and IV on the Serb side and Dobrinja II and III on the Muslim side. That is where the nearest contact was. At times there was just a street separating them. In some places there were buildings on the opposite sides. And there were also instances when both parties would be in one and the same building. There was movement only under the cover of darkness, and if somebody noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am sorry for interrupting you. I do not want you to sum up what you told us yesterday, but I'm asking you what can you tell us about what went on between the opposed positions regarding the fire between -- the exchange of fire, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire was opened -- fire would be opened if a soldier of the other side emerged somewhere, be it in daytime or at night. If somebody started moving openly, since this was the line of direct contact, there were no warnings nor would one wait for orders to open fire, and both parties opened fire whenever the enemy -- whenever an enemy soldier would emerge in view.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, immediately after that question that you were asked by Judge Nieto-Navia, you showed us the north-north-west part of the airport, and you indicated with your hand where that was. However, it was not clear, at least not to me, what you meant by that. What was it that you meant when you mentioned the north-north-west part of the airport? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed that the runway extended in north -- towards north-west, that is, towards Ilidza. And our signs were -- our forces were in the -- in its north-eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, following a question asked by Judge El Mahdi, you said that eventually the air warfare started. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, my question is as follows: How many -- how efficient -- how efficient was the positioning of the batteries, such as it was at that time, concerning strictly speaking the anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions were good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As the witness himself indicated, that postdates the relevant period, and therefore the question lacks relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. If the witness would take off his earphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, because the position is as follows -- may I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a relatively technical matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position is as follows: We are not trying to speak about when the air warfare started in Bosnia-Herzegovina effectively, but the purpose of the question, at least why the positioning was taking place. People do not know when air war is going to be declared under those circumstances. What is interesting to find out is whether the positioning of the battery, such as it was, around Sarajevo was conceived within the framework of anti-aircraft defence and not in some other -- within some other framework, and that applies to the period under consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you answer the question -- now, please, will you put on your headset. Yes. Witness, do you remember the question, and will you answer it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions of the units that I spoke about of the anti-aircraft defence were appropriate with certain shifts for the performance of tasks in those areas where there were operations. After the period that we are talking about, that is, after August 1994, during this period of time and later on we also carried out the training of units which were involved with the force system Strela 2M, and that is light equipment and they had their moving positions for them, that is, they made part of the large units previously deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I now want to move on to a series of questions that were asked by Judge Orie. Do you remember that you were asked about the state hospital? And I want to ask you something about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us regarding the destruction of the state hospital, that is, the facade of the hospital facing Vrace in chronological terms, if you can do that? That is, do you remember when did the major part of this damage happen? What do you know about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer cannot be complete in this case because I said yesterday that the state hospital, that is, the military hospital, was not one of the objectives -- one of the targets that was under my or my unit's jurisdiction, that it was not for us an interesting target, and that it could have been hit by accident. I can tell you confidently and sincerely that I never paid any attention and that from Vrace I didn't even try to see what the upper storeys of the state hospital looked like, and that is why I said that I assumed that only the top part of the building could be seen. So I really am not able to tell you how badly the building was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like us now to broach what we call Christmas fire or Christmas shots. My first question is: What was the chief religion in the units for which you were responsible? Which was for the most part the religion embraced by your units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the units for which I was responsible, people were Orthodox, were of Eastern Orthodox faith. In our units, we had one or two Muslims even or Croats, but apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you remind us for the sake of clarity what is the date of Christmas adhering to this faith?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Took all measures not to sit on Christmas -- Orthodox Christmas. I think it's really something that is well known to the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, since we all know --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, very much. And we thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why should then an unit which was almost exclusively Orthodox to celebrate on the 24th something, since that was not its holiday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason at all. I've already said that. Because in the immediate context --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Thank you. I now move on to what you told us, and you told us that you had trouble with ammunition. If we're talking about 20 minutes of incessant fire, in view of the weapons which were explicitly mentioned, that is, all the artillery weapons, including the tank, including the AAD weaponry, can you tell us approximately what would be the quantity of the necessary ammunition to allow incessant fire from all these pieces for something that amounts to 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 40-millimetre gun in 20 minutes can fire -- or rather, any piece can use up and complete a set and spend all it bullets at a position which would never occur to anyone, the platoon commander, a foot soldier, a gunner, or anyone. As for other pieces, in 20 minutes' time, all these pieces would have used up all their ammunition stocks, and I would have used up all the available ammunition at a particular position in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please wait for the witness to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, all these pieces of artillery around Sarajevo, had they opened their fire and kept firing for 20 minutes, can you tell us from the logistics point of view how many trucks would have been needed to carry all this ammunition around Sarajevo. Can you tell us an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about my pieces. 8.000 bullets, one battery can fire 8.000 bullets in less than 20 minutes. In other words, a 110-tonne truck with these 8.000 bullets which are fired in less than 20 minutes with a change of the drum. In other words, of the ammunition available, if I had planned three combat sets, then I'd need a truck per battery, which makes for three trucks. So only I, that is, my unit, would need for these six or seven batteries -- we'd practically need 20 trucks to transport just one set of ammunition per battery. Not to speak of brigades which are much stronger and which have many more pieces. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps did not have that many trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let us imagine, witness, that other sectors of armament - and I'm still talk hypothetically - that they also needed and used the same quantity of ammunition, and again I'm still talking approximately. They would need about the same number of trucks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, artillery perhaps would need more. I'm sure about that. And tanks would need even more, because a tank cannot carry too much ammunition, so they need accompanying trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, witness, in view of your position --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to this line of questioning, although your questions to the witness at one point concerned the events of Christmas, it was not this aspect. And indeed, it was open to my learned colleague in re-examination following my cross-examination to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I asked a series of important questions dealing both with the Orthodox and the Catholic Christmas, and you asked those questions, and you asked the witness about this, to clarify a number of points. Now, I believe the Defence is entitled to ask because we never asked about these types of rounds of fire, what does -- what do 20 minutes of fire mean for all the pieces around in Sarajevo, and we believe that we're entitled to ask these questions and clarify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has answered, at least, the first of your questions, and it appears that his testimony is that it would take -- this intensity of firing of all the units and batteries would take such an immense logistical exercise. And he gave examples of what would be needed only for his units. So I think what the witness tells us in this respect is quite clear. But if you have one or more two questions -- I mean, that -- the line of his answer is perfectly clear, and I don't think that mathematics on all the units would be necessary in order to understand his testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes. It's along those lines, one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since this logistics - and again, I'm saying hypothetically - also would imply orders which would be issued and transmitted, did you ever at any moment around the date of the -- around the date of the 24th December 1992 and then on the 6th of January, 1993, did you ever see any such order that would be of this nature, that is, which would have to do with the order and supply of a major quantity of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. President, I'd like us to throw more light on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I want to see if you remember a particular thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'd like to have on the ELMO a document which is numbered 05958985 [as interpreted], and I have a copy for everybody, and it is only a document which is an UNPROFOR document, that is, a document which originated with military observers themselves. It is only a few lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I seek --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I see the document before it's placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is a document -- it is Exhibit P620. It was tendered under number P620, and I have here one page of the document and I'm interested only in page 9 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there have been tight constraints on the examination of this witness exercised by the Trial Chamber. This line of questioning clearly goes beyond the issues that you raised with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. I have not yet looked at this document, so I don't know whether there's a -- a direct relation to that. But Mr. -- You say, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're only interested in page 9. Could you tell us which part, because there appear to be different dates on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is very important because you yourself asked questions of what the witness remembered while he was on Trebevic. He told you he didn't remember. And this is the 24th December 1992. And again, I'll read it to you, because that would not be right. But it tells us very clearly about a number of shots fired and registered by military observers. And if there are any doubts, we also have the date of the 25th of December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see that the document directly relates to the 24th of December, 1992. It says in the top that it's a confidential document. Is it still, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was tendered in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was never tendered or admitted. P620 is not on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, my apologies. We have it with seal P620, but perhaps it was withdrawn. I apologise. I see here the stamp of the Prosecution, but perhaps it was not tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you -- perhaps you first check that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no idea at this moment what exactly document it is. Is the Prosecution aware of what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I first raise this issue, that at the moment we are in open session. The witness has his headphones on. Mr. Piletta-Zanin is indicating in part, at least, the contents of the document, that it's an entirely inappropriate way for us to be dealing with the admissibility of the document or the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree. I limited it myself that it was about the 24th of December. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you explained extensively where the document came from, what it was about. That's not a proper way of describing a document when it still has to be introduced to a witness, because it's of no use to ask him questions on that any more because he has heard perhaps part of the answers already. Could you please at this very moment move to your next subject and we'll consider what to do, whether any questions will be allowed on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I should be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let me say something. I wanted to confront the memory of the witness about what is said in this document, and I do not have the impression that I was in breach of any regulations or rules that we have to comply with. But I will move on to another subject, and I believe that I will have to opportunity to come back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will consider whether additional questions. And perhaps you'll find out in the meanwhile what creates the confusion as to whether this is admitted or tendered document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to opening fire, you said that when something was being celebrated on the balcony, it was customary on occasion to fire. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In such a situation, when one fires, can you tell us what one fires at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into the air. Into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yesterday you used the term "making a lot of noise." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you used this term, when you said "making a loud noise," were you referring to the same thing that you mentioned a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, firing into the air, to mark something, to celebrate something. There was no particular purpose -- no particular reason to fire at a specific target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that is in relation to the answer that you provided yesterday; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, around the 24th or 25th of December, 1992, do you know whether there was a fairly large-scale military operation that was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't believe you've ruled on my objection against this line of questioning which goes well beyond the specific issue that you raised in your questions of the witness, which was whether from where he was he could have heard such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to the issue of complaints and firing incidents. You mentioned in general terms - I don't have the page. It was yesterday - you mentioned investigations carried out by those who were responsible for this, investigations into firing incidents, to prove that these protests didn't correspond to reality. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you be more specific and tell us what you mean when you say that this did not correspond to the truth or to reality. Could you please be more specific and provide us with more details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the case of Dobrinja. On the first day a protest was lodged, and through the media it was stated that no conclusions had been reached, neither by members of the corps who participated in the investigation of the case nor by UNPROFOR representatives. And finally, that protest wasn't confirmed by the opposing side either. So the media would step ahead and say lots of things and that was ascribed to us. These protests were investigated, but it was most often the case that the protests were not confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, could you take note of the following, what you said in your testimony yesterday, with regard to the problem of what we call small arms here, or rather, infantry arms. You said the following, and I am going to quote you from the English transcript: [In English] -- Whether a team was formed on every occasion because it was mostly combat operations." Do you remember this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What I'm interested in are the terms that you used. And I'll repeat them: [In English] "combat operations." [Interpretation] What did you mean by that? What did you want to indicate when you said that it was mostly combat operations? Could you please expand on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be as brief as possible, when I used the term "combat operation," I think that the protest might have had sense when there was a cease-fire, when there was a so-called truth. That's why I said "mostly," because there were mostly combat operations but there were several such violations and there were casualties. I know that there were a lot of casualties on our side too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But I think that for me personally the answer isn't quite clear. I'll rephrase the question. What are the risks, if any, for the civilian population in the situation that you described as a military operation? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. The civilian population was always at risk if they moved in the area or the immediate vicinity of the contact line and the combat area. It was possible for something to happen, for there to be casualties at the most peaceful place outside the combat zone. So no one could guarantee in the area and in the line of contact and in the zone of combat, no one could guarantee safety for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And why would someone have been killed in an area that was peaceful or relatively peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I respectfully submit these questions go well beyond the line of questioning by you and Your Honours. I'd be grateful for some guidance as to whether you wish me to raise what I would think to be appropriate objections or whether given that the questioning came from you and Your Honours, you take the view that you don't want that assistance and it's for you and Your Honours to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I maintain that this arises directly from the answer that this witness provided to your question with regard to the question of the investigations carried out. The witness quite clearly said what the case was with regard to combat situations for most of the time. He's just provided some important information with regard to the calm areas, calm zones. I think it is our responsibility to clarify this, whether we like it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question put to the witness may be answered by the witness. This does not mean that you're not at the edge of what was the subject of my questioning. Please proceed. And so the question was why people -- why someone would have been killed in an area that was peaceful or relatively peaceful. You yourself, you talked about places outside of the zone of combat. Would you tell us how -- why someone would be killed there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the area near the line of contact, the combat area, can have a depth. It varies. Civilians could be at risk in an area of 100 or 200 metres or in an area of 2 kilometres or more. The conditions weren't such, and I think this is the case for the enemy side too. It wasn't possible to move all the population for each combat -- move out all the population for each combat operation. The entire Sarajevo would have had to have been moved out and all the surrounding villages. They would have had to move them 5 kilometres from the line of contact, and this was impossible. No decree or instructions from a president of any state couldn't do that, so it means that civilians on both sides, many of them found themselves in the combat zone. If the effective range of a rifle is 700 metres, a bullet which misses its target could represent a threat for a civilian at a range of 3 kilometres into the depth. A civilian could be digging in the garden in front of his or her house, and there were such cases where civilians died. And this relates to a distance of up to 2 kilometres in the depth, and it could be a danger for children too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about Markale. You answered certain questions about Markale. I'm referring to the explosion, or rather, the problem of Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, questions have been put to the witness not about Markale itself but about discussions about Markale and the basis for such discussions. Investigations, discussions, but not the content of the Markale incident itself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just confer for a minute. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Provided certain details about Markale, do you have any other information that you could provide to this Trial Chamber in order to clarify the matter completely? That would be my very last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. And whether any subsequent questions can be put to him in relation to his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: May I be heard, Mr. President, in relation to the objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I thought I understood it. But perhaps I am not listening carefully enough. Could your objection be raised in the presence of the witness, or would we have to -- could the objection be explained? It has been raised already.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Might he be taken from the courtroom, Mr. President and the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness for a minute out of the courtroom. Mr. DP35, I have to ask you to take off the headphones and to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, your questioning about Markale was a probing of what internal investigation was carried out by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. This question by Mr. Piletta-Zanin is extraordinarily broad, the keyword being "do you have any other information that you could provide to this Trial Chamber." They're the keywords. The topic, Markale. It's an indication to the witness to say whatever he likes about Markale in terms of hearsay, any aspect of Markale. That's not at all -- question does not at all focus the attention of the witness. And for this question to be asked after re-examination following on questions by Your Honours which touched on one aspect of Markale, that is an internal SRK investigation, in my respectful submission creates a problem. If this is permissible, then it means that any topic raised by questions from the Bench can then be the subject of further re-examination, in terms of any other aspect. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what did you have in mind when you put the question to the witness whether he had any additional information about Markale?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I didn't want to interrupt, but I think that this witness, when he answered the question, I don't think the witness provided detailed information about what he may have known about the UN's reaction to the investigation that was carried out. He spoke in very general terms, but he didn't go into details. And I think that given the rank of this witness, it would be useful to hear what he has to say. But the issue is for you to decide. Mr. President, may I use this time while the witness is absent and just point out another problem, the 24th and 25th of December and the 6th of January, 1992 and 1993. Could I mention -- could I discuss this very briefly before the witness returns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd just like to -- to ask you a clarification of what you just said. You said that you don't think that the witness provided detailed information about what he may have known about the UN's reaction to the investigation. That raises a few questions. The first is whether he has been asked about the UN reaction to the investigation. And it's not clear to me what you mean by "the investigation." Do you mean one of the five, six, or seven investigations that we have heard about or any other investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the investigations carried out by the United Nations and that we are familiar with here, and I'm referring to the reactions of some members of the UN with regard to the quality of these investigations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The questions put to the witness by the Bench related to whatever investigation done by the Bosnian Serb forces, not by any other institution. So questions are allowed in relation to any investigation done by the Bosnian Serb forces, not any other investigation. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the second issue you wanted to raise was about the -- another problem about Christmas -- Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: May that be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The next one to be done in private session, you'd say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The discussion about the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that -- this report, yes. We could do that in private session. Could we turn in to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to Markale, do you know whether there was an investigations team that was formed at the level of the general staff in order to examine the situation and the cause, if any, and if such a team -- commission was formed, what could you tell us about it? Who participated in its work and what were the relations, if any, of this commission with other parties, other commissions, et cetera? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if a commission was formed at the level of the general staff because I didn't have any documents that had to do with that. I know that there was an order and I know what I said in my previous answers. I know that it was suggested that a team should be formed which was to participate in a joint commission at the level of the corps. But about the general staff, I can't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like to read something out to you very briefly, which is the description provided by certain authorities about the shelling dated the 24th of December, 1992. And I'm going to read it out to you. Could you please listen to what I'm going to read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, could we hand out this document to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, the mere fact that the document reads confidential at the top, is that any reason -- because I do not see that it has got an R number, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There's no objection from the Prosecution to it being used in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may the document be put on the ELMO, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read this document out to you. And I would be grateful if you could concentrate on its contents. For the 24th of December, 1992, I am going to quote the following in English. [In English] "A relatively quiet day with 14 rounds incoming to Presidency side and 82 rounds incoming to Serb side. Total rounds recorded outgoing from Serb positions 3, from Presidency positions, 14," [Interpretation] et cetera. This is the only part we are interested in. We are interested in what you can remember. As far as you can remember, the sound of shots on Sarajevo as a whole at that time, does this official description seem to correspond more exactly to what you can remember? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've understood the question. On that day I was in Trebevic. And whether there was noise caused by opening fire, well, I can't remember, just as I can't remember the event itself. And what you have just read out to me is not information that reached me. I don't know whether a protest was lodged and this is probably an UNPROFOR record about what happened on that day, according to what you have informed me of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Is there any need to put further questions on the basis of what -- of questions of the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. This concludes your examination, but nevertheless we'd like you to stay until after the break and the Chamber would like to receive from the parties during the break the whole of the document of which a part was just read out. So if the parties could provide that -- one of the parties, the most -- who has this document nearest by to present the whole of this document to the Chamber so that we can have a look at it. If this would cause us to ask any additional questions to the witness, it would be done after the break. So therefore, I'd like you to return even if it would be just for one or two minutes or even if it would be just to tell you that there are no further questions to you after the break. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please first escort the witness into the courtroom. The Chamber will have no further questions for the witness, but we'd like to tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst that's occurring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- If you wish it, I can give the page references of Carl Harding and Pyers Tucker for the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have -- of course it would certainly assist. But if you would like me to read part of it, it's already in front of me. If you give them, then the Defence is saved additional time to search for it. So if you have got them available, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to Pyers Tucker, military attache to General Morillon, in terms of the Microsoft word transcript, it's pages 9923 through to 9927. In relation to Carl Harding, the Papa subcommander, the page references are 4375 through to 4378. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. DP35, the Chamber has no further questions for you. We are aware that you have been in this courtroom for quite some time and you had to answer a lot of questions, both from the parties and from the Bench. I thank you very much for coming your long way to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In respect of the documents the Chamber has just asked for, in order to assist the Chamber in finding support or contradiction in documentary evidence, the parties, whether it's the Defence or the Prosecution - it's not of major importance - are invited to produce the whole of the senior military observers end-of-month report of December and of January, and in addition those pages of annex 6 to the report of the committee of experts dealing with the period of the 22nd of January until the 8th of -- 22nd of December, 1992 until the 8th of January, 1993. Then there would be no need, I take it, to tender page 9 out of 13, because that's part of the documents the Chamber now requires to be produced by the parties. Madam Registrar, apart from these documents that have not -- we asked for that have not yet been numbered, I take it that the parties -- or should they receive a number, a C number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties certainly when meeting one of these days can decide who's going to produce them and tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't think much depends on which side tenders it as long as it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Then we're happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just for the Chamber, as long as we have access to it. It's just for the parties as long as we have access to it and can look at it. Could you please assist us in respect of the other document, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D8 -- D1828, under seal, pseudonym sheet; Exhibit D1829, hand-drawn diagram, Brdo Mojmilo; Exhibit D1830, map marked by witness; Exhibit D1491, report SRK command dated 03/04/1993; and D1491.1, English translation; D1492 under seal, report from SRK command dated 15 September 1993; D1492.1 under seal, English translation; D1493, report SRK command dated 11 August 1993; D1493.1, English translation; D1494, report dated 23/02/1992; D1494.1, English translation; Exhibit P3770 under seal, B/C/S report SRK command dated 9 April 1993; P3770.1, English translation; P3771, black-and-white photocopies of photographs of various weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber hears no objections, these documents are admitted into evidence, under seal as indicated by Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would it be convenient to tender those further documents at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they're there, if they're numbered. It could be done -- if it would be done on Monday, that's fine as well. I don't know whether we have the annexes to the report. We asked for a relatively long period of time, 22nd of December until the 8th of January, I think I said. We have until now just the beginning of January, and we'd like to have it for the whole of the period, although it's even if the whole bunch of documents would be ready as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respectfully suggest that that date be extended to the 14th of January so as to cover the 13th, which I think is the Serbian New Year. There's a relevant entry for the 13th of January in the monthly report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President, for the simple reason that we never asked that this witness - and he's just been released - concerning the Serbian New Year. We were asking him questions about the Catholic Christmas and Serb Christmas, and as the case may be, but we never had a single question referring to the 13th of January. And I do not think that anybody could accept this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These documents are not introduced through a witness, as you might have noticed. But Mr. Ierace, before giving a decision on that, could you please respond to -- is there one -- as I said, the Chamber was seeking this documentary evidence in order to make it possible for the Chamber to seek any support or contradiction on any -- on any testimony about this type of events. Could you indicate whether there would be any mentioning of New Year's Eve -- Orthodox New Year's Eve, the 13th, because it's not clearly in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the monthly report of January, which I think you have a copy of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Your Honours will see a comment that it's anticipated that there may be activity -- excuse me. I'll go straight to the reference. Yes. I could read out the comment or it's a matter for Your Honours to read it, but it appears on page 4 under the date of the 13th of January. But Mr. President, given your earlier invitation was -- or requirement was in relation to the annexes, I assume that's the annexes to the expert's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have, in any event, the monthly report, so I think that's probably sufficient -- for the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no -- you withdraw the extension.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So would then the annexes -- annex 6 should then cover the period of the 22nd of December until the 8th of January. If the documents are fully available, especially the annex until now as we received it from the Defence a few minutes ago is not covering the whole period we asked for, if the documents are fully available, we'll then decide on -- there are three of the documents to be admitted into evidence. Then is the Defence ready to call its next witness? And I think we still first have to discuss an application made in respect of that witness. And perhaps we should then turn into closed session for that reason. Yes. We'll then turn in to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. DP36, you are now at the beginning of your testimony. And the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be first examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP36, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we start the examination of the witness, we shall show the witness a document and ask the witness to tell us whether the information on the sheet of paper is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer the question of Ms. Pilipovic, whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is the information in this document accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, everything is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see a face which I do not know in the public gallery, and that is why I am interrupting, even if this is not my custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against faces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am informed that this is one of the legal assistants of the Chamber who is attending. But I might have another problem. Ms. Pilipovic, I take it, then, that you -- is that acceptable? We could actually return to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I simply wanted to check this. I wasn't -- I didn't want to offend anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're perfectly right, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It's -- protective measures have to be taken very seriously. I do, however, have another problem. I take it that while asking the witness whether the information was correct or not you didn't ask him to verify the number used for this witness. It was just indicated to us that it was DP36, and I find a different number on the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard that. Your Honour, I did say -- I said that he was DP35 -- that is, 36. Perhaps there was a mistake in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now again you say "36," but on the piece of paper it says "34." And thus --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what this is about. I once again say that I said "34," and the general says that he also heard this. This is why I don't understand what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now for the first time in translation we hear that it's 34. So until now I addressed you by the wrong name, that is, DP36, and I should have addressed you by DP34. I don't know whether that feels any better, but -- Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for the mistakes. Your Honour, in order to obtain more detailed information about witness DP34, perhaps it would be a good idea to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn in to private session, as we usually do in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, you said that the official foundation of your brigade was in September 1992 but that it also existed prior to that date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes, it did exist as a formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when it first came into existence of as formation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, as a military unit I have to be a little more specific so that you can understand this -- it existed from the beginning of the war. But the fact that it was called a brigade is more a psychological matter, you know. There was also an operations group at the time and the brigade was part of it. That's also a psychological issue, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, thank you. When you say that it existed as a unit but that it was called a brigade and that this was a psychological matter, can you tell us when it was formed as a unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Officially it was formed when the superior command established it in official terms and stamped it, gave it a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But as a unit --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, from the beginning of the war. I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was formed as a unit at the beginning of the war and you said that that was on the 4th of April, 1992, can you tell us how this took place. How was it formed and who became part of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, it happened spontaneously. It was founded spontaneously, and the local inhabitants became part of the unit, the local inhabitants from those local areas which was within the zone of responsibility of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say "the local inhabitants from those areas." How many such local areas were there that became part of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: When I say "the local areas," to be more clear these were local communes which in the former system existed as social and political organisations. You know, these were the local communes of Mrkovici, Pionirska Dolina, the local commune of Betanija and the local commune of Nahorevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- Mr. DP34, could you please repeat the names of the local communes. You said Mrkovici, Pionirska Dolina, Betanija, and Nahorevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what the problem is. It hasn't entered the transcript again, but we can correct that later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be re-listened at at night, and it certainly will appear properly by tomorrow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, you said that that unit was formed and that the local inhabitants became part of the unit. Can you tell us why the inhabitants organised themselves and formed such a unit in that area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, the well-known events that preceded that period, the period of March and the beginning of April, during that time it's a well-known fact that many dangerous things happened. Barricades had been set up throughout the town. People would be stopped, searched. Cars would be searched. There was physical maltreatment, et cetera. There was separation along ethnic lines. You are familiar with this. And groups were formed in local communes or in neighbourhoods on this basis and that's how everything began.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the area that you have mentioned and where you say people got together, can you tell us whether there was a specific incident in that area that occurred and in a certain way put the inhabitants of that area at risk. Did anything specific take place in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, yes, in that area, and I can be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is all pre-indictment period, and the Prosecution objects on relevance grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is there any -- did you have any specific incident in mind which has not been object of testimony several times? Apart from relevance, we accept that the -- is of some relevance. But the other issue I would like to raise is whether this part of the evidence is repetitious. So if we would hear about events we heard about many times and if we would hear about events on which the Prosecution hardly ever cross-examined, then it might become repetitious. So please keep this in mind and then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But I just have to say that I think I was precise. I only mentioned this area, and I think that this is a witness who is now testifying about this area. He is the first witness to testify about this area. That's why I put this question to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, in the area you lived in, in the area of those local communes of yours when the local inhabitants organised themselves in a spontaneous manner, as you said, did some specific incident occur which in a certain way put the inhabitants at risk and incited you to organise yourselves spontaneously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, because of these objections, I will mention a specific example. On the 6th of April, 1992 there was a murder at the area where two local communes joined, Mrkovici and Pionirska Dolina. There was a murder. Perhaps the same thing happened in Sarajevo. Nedjo Dragas was murdered in the Mrkovici area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who killed that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992 in the afternoon an attack was carried out from the direction of the Panjina Kula local commune in the direction of the Mrkovici local commune. And this murder took place in the course of the attack. I said I would attempt to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the witness was asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I can see that in the English transcript part of the witness's answer does not appear with regard to the ethnic composition of a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again ask you to slow down a bit, Mr. DP34, because you're speaking rather quickly and the interpreters cannot follow that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll attempt to do so. I really will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see anything as to the ethnic composition of a village. So if you said something about that, would you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't, but I know for sure, since that is the neighbouring local commune --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you didn't say it, it's not necessary to -- Please put your next question to the witness, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, you said that Nedjo Dragas was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the ethnic composition of the inhabitants of the area where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: It was exclusively Serbian before the war, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that an attack was carried out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Against your area. You said from the Panjina Kula local commune.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes, from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From that direction. Thank you. Can you tell us who carried the attack out? Who carried the attack out against your local communes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: That was a military formation. I don't know whether it was the Army of the Federation, as it was called later, or the Patriotic League, or some police unit. It's not possible to identify this precisely, but it was a formation which had the strength of a company. And it was armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP34, you spoke about your unit. Can you tell us who the men in your unit were, those who were fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, it was a very specific unit from the beginning to the end of the war. Perhaps a little unusual -- this was perhaps a little unusual, but it consisted of all those who were fit for military service, all those who considered themselves to be fit for military service, so that means those who were younger than 18 and over 60. And in addition, there was a large number of women who joined the unit on a voluntary basis, but they weren't conscripts, about 150 of them -- 151, I think, in fact, to be more precise. That's how many women there were in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, can you tell us whether you were armed, and if you were, what kind of weapons did you have, and how did you arm yourselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: At the beginning, we were partially armed. And as the war advanced, our weapons became better and better. But when we finished arming ourselves, well, that was around August 1992. At the beginning we had our personal weapons, hunting weapons, weapons from the reserve police forces. Some people would obtain weapons -- purchase weapons through various channels. We got a lot of weapons from the Territorial Defence, from the Faletici warehouse. An important amount of weapons came from that warehouse. And later on in May and June we also received weapons from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that this period went up until July, which is when you received better weapons -- slightly better weapons. Can you tell us -- if I've understood you correctly, you gradually armed yourselves. Can you tell us whether it was necessary to arm yourselves in this gradual manner and whether any -- was anything happening in that area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, it's not that it was necessary, but there was a lot of pressure. The population was asking -- they were asking each other for weapons. They were trying to find a way of obtaining weapons, of buying weapons. People would give a cow for a rifle and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, the reason was the event, the incident that occurred. I said that on the 6th the first murder occurred. And then later on there were permanent attacks carried out against that area and they were very intense for the first three months. Almost -- they occurred almost on a daily basis. And in the course of 24 hours, there would be several such attacks, you know. And during that period there were casualties. People were wounded, and there were people who were killed. But that unit had the greatest number of casualties in average terms in the first half of 1992. This is when it had the greatest number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say "in the first half of 1992." You say that fighting was most intense at that time, it took place on an almost daily basis, and that's when you had the greatest number of casualties of wounded and dead. Can you tell us which period that is exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: That is from the month of April, May, June, and July. From the 31st of July, there was a lull in the attacks. The number of attacks diminished. But the intensity of the attacks -- as far as the intensity is concerned, there were other intense attacks. But as far as the number of attacks is concerned, the number diminished. So this happened most frequently in those first four months.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I show you a map so that you can mark that area on the map, the area that you are talking about, you've mentioned intense attacks, large-scale attacks. In relation to the area where your unit was located, can you tell us which direction these attacks were carried out from in the direction of your houses and positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: There were frontal attacks in front of our front lines from part of the municipality which was in the hands of the other side. We had the northern part. So that means that the attacks came from the south, the direction of the south, the direction of the town, and from the flanks, but always from the direction of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During that period that you have referred to when the attacks were very intense, can you tell us what sort of weapons the other side used against you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, they used infantry weapons. The weapons they had were similar to the ones that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has part of a map. And to ensure that everything is clear, we would like the witness to mark the area he is talking about on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the number is P1834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I do not mind if -- but where I earlier asked you to look carefully that there would be no repetitious evidence, you indicated that this was the first witness to talk about this area, and I understood also that this would be the first witness to talk about the event that you asked him. May I remind you that we have some evidence also in respect of the event you just mentioned. For example, I remember that Mr. Nikolic was testifying about the attack in which Nedjo Dragas was killed. So I do not mind. But where I asked you to avoid repetitious evidence, you answered that it was totally new. I just want to bring to your attention that that was not correct as in respect of the question you then put to the witness. So would you please keep this in mind. I will not interfere any more with the -- the questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would just like to say that the gentleman whose name you mentioned was a protected witness. Perhaps that should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he was -- oh, yes. Perhaps that's -- yes. It should be redacted. I apologise, and thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to show the map to the witness. Could you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, if possible could you use a black felt-tip to mark the area of the zone of responsibility of your unit. And later on I will put some questions to you. For the sake of the transcript, could you tell us what area this is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: It's elevation 103 including the Slatina direction, the Slatina -- just a minute. And then the fence of the zoo in the direction of - just a minute - towards Kosevo stream, you cross the Kosevo stream at the Sutjeska Film bridge and then you go along Breka - just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps the map be moved a bit on the ELMO and zoomed in a bit so we can better follow what the witness actually marks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards elevation 906 exclusive. There was a house here, so-called Kadina Kuca, Kadina house, and that's where the 1st Romanija Brigade was located. That's what it looked like. Elevation 703, inclusive. Elevation 906, exclusive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So this area, the line that you drew eastward from the word "Brijeg," above the word "703," above the words Kobilja Glava, then the line goes through which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Betanija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Betanija. Horizontally towards feature 806.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: No, not 806 but 906. Because there was a forest here and we were below it. And from there the 1st Romanija Brigade took over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I interrupt you. You just have drawn my attention that Vaso Nikolic was a protected witness and I apologised for it and asked you for correcting me. I now checked. I took it that if you make such a comment that the basis is just as precise as any comment you made on whether the event was the subject of testimony before and that whatever information you give exactly on the return of property of a witness that that is also precise and correct information. It turned out not to be. So where I indicated that a redaction would be made, I now have to withdraw that. Vaso Nikolic was not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: May I -- I can see better here, but it is not precise 100 per cent. I mean, the map is not quite accurate. But it is more or less that, plus/minus 100 metres north-south, I mean. Now, on the monitor I could see better some houses which were our houses and which I omitted here, but I do not think it really matters. That is the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, can you tell us how long was the line - to call it that - of the front of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, if we measured the length of the trenches, that is, not as the crow flies, it was 7 kilometres long. Of course, as the crow flies, it would be shorter. But the trenches were -- zigzagged a great deal. And if you straighten them out, then that is how long they would be, and it is shorter as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you are mentioning the trenches, can you tell us when were the trenches dug.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The trenches were dug as early as April. And the line as a whole was established in -- the end of the May already, and all the engineering works were completed by the end of June. That is, by that time the trenches were dug, all the engineering security and everything else was done. So we did it step by step. But first we simply started building basic trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP34, can you tell us how far were the positions of the adversary in relation to the positions of your unit? And if you can, mark them with a blue dotted line -- no, sorry, black marker but dotted line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yeah, sure. Of course I can. So it's like this. This is the first line. Can I correct this now. It could be like this. Like that. Then here in this area, they were almost -- they came almost together. That is, there was less than 50 metres between them here. Then up here, it was like this more or less. So the separation line between us and the enemy was 50 to 250 metres. In places, for instance, where the area was quite open, it could be as much as 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the positions of your unit, can you tell us and can you show on this map -- but first tell us, were there troops at the positions and where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Do you mean the soldiers of the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yours, the positions of your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The soldiers were in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the depth of your area of -- of your brigade's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: About 5 kilometres deep northward. From the line that I drew, then northward, about 5 kilometres deep. But these are all habitable houses. Actually, in this area there are many more houses and that is where the soldiers were accommodated because there were no conventional barracks. That is where they lived and then they would go -- come here to the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the soldiers of your unit lived in houses which were in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, some of the houses were near the line and there were bunkers, and that is how they served until the end of the war. I'm referring to this peak here, to this peak above the former Jezero hospital and here the Breka Potok -- there were streets -- sorry, houses which were practically the last line of defence. And on the houses of these buildings we had made several openings to be able to fire from them. And the same held true of the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you point at the map, would you please do it at the map on the right-hand side because we cannot see what you point at on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I realise that I made a mistake. So the lines were the closest here. You can hear it like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you another thing: Would you please only mark something on the map if you're specifically requested to do so. So if you point at something, use the pointer, not the pen. And if someone asks you to mark something on the map, then you use the pen in the colour indicated. Yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, before -- before you answered, I think that the end of your answer was the same held true of the other side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: In this part here --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just take it easy. When you say "on the other side," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, you can see here that there were houses here on both sides and that they were nearby. You can't see it here because this is an old map but there were very many houses here. And what I mean is that in this part here -- in this part here that we were in houses and the adversary side was also in houses. That is what I meant. Here. And over here -- up here there were trenches. They had their trenches, and we had our own trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you are talking about the enemy side and when you're talking about the trenches of the enemy side and the length of the front line in relation to yours, can you tell us if you had any information, you personally, about which unit was the enemy unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: According to our intelligence, directly in front of the line, that is, in the centre of the city, was the 105th Brigade. And on our left flank we had -- that is, in front of our left flank was the 2nd, and in front of the right flank, in front of Vogosca was the 15th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you could find a suitable moment for a break either now or within a couple of minutes, then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can do it now, Mr. President, because we've covered this area, regarding the front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn until quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, on the map that we were looking at before the break and that we were talking about, you drew the lines of your and the adversary army's positions and you told us what are the units across from the position of your units called. Can you tell us, from September 1992 until August 1994, did those lines shift? On both sides, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
