utterances.text: Yes. There were some insignificant microshifts. But generally speaking, this is the line. They were very slight shifts of technical -- of tactical significance on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you personally tell us about this line as you drew it, that is, of both sides? When was it finally established? Which month of which year when this line was established such as it was and after which only some tactical movements were? Can you tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you that. As a line, organised in this form existed from the very beginning, and some three months after its establishment, after its final establishment, it was fully structured -- I mean, all the engineering works were completed and the moves happened in 1993. Only slight. Here in the area of Betanija and here there were some insignificant shifts. And here towards feature 906, it never changed at all. There is a watershed here, or rather, there is a brook here which is called the Breka potok which dries up in summer but does have water in winter and it was a kind of boundary. So this part, the western part, the right flank of the Kosevo Brigade and this peak here, this is where the shifts occurred but they were completely insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DP34. Mr. DP34, you told us that throughout the conflict - and we're speaking about September 1992/August 1994 - that throughout that period of time you had a commanding position in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have some more precise --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I said that the Kosevo Brigade existed until February, until the 1st of February, 1994. And you are mentioning the period of August 1994. I was not the commander of the Kosevo Brigade any longer because it stopped existing as the Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you held this duty until February 1994; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about that period while you were the commander, can you tell us if you cooperated with UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. From the time when UNPROFOR forces arrived to the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, or more precisely the Sarajevo Kosevo Brigade, we maintained contact with UNPROFOR members and to my mind they were both very successful on both sides. I think UNPROFOR members were very satisfied, and I was more than satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that area, in your area, did they have their observation post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was their observation post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Let me say first that in the early days they had their observers who came and went, and the place where they eventually stationed for a longer period is the area -- just a minute. This is the area of Pretrzanj where artillery was. Just a moment. It's up here. Right here. Exactly. That is where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point at it again because it was just moved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pretrzanj. Saracevac feature 1080 is north of it. So it's right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, will you make a circle and put number "1" there so that for the transcript we could say that the area -- the word is Pretrzanj and it needs to be precise. The first four letters of the word Pretrzanj, the witness has circled it and put number "1" to mark the observation post of the UNPROFOR and about a place that the witness says it was where artillery was positioned. And according to the witness's explanation, this observation post is south of feature number 1080.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Saracevac

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34 when you tell us that your cooperation with UNPROFOR was correct and that they had their observation post, I will come back to this and ask you some further questions about the cooperation that existed between you. But before that I'd like you to answer whether you had any information, whether they, that is, UNPROFOR members, keep their maps with marked positions of your brigade and whether -- were you aware of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. They had their own maps, topographic maps which looked slightly different from our maps because we were using maps of the Army of Yugoslavia, that is, issued by the publisher in Belgrade. And I've forgotten the rest of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is what I asked you. Now I will show you three maps, which will be D1835. And they are annexes to document number 6. Page 1278, three maps. I have them for the -- I have copies for the witness and for the Chamber and for the adversary's side, if I may call it that. I have enough copies, but I did not copy the same format. But all these three maps are both for the Chamber and for the Prosecution. D1385. Sorry, 1835. Something is wrong with me today obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, let's -- will you put this map on the ELMO. Can you tell us if you recognise areas on this map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in the right corner of the map, at the bottom of the map, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: You mean in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The date, 12th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you take up the marker -- up the pointer, excuse me, and tell us what these lines on the map mean, those black lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The black lines are the lines of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the lines of the Federation, of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is, they show the boundary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, so you're telling us -- can you use the pointer to point at your brigade's positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. However the scale is not particularly good. It's not very precise, but it's this part, 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you pull the map down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, this is it. This is what I drew a moment ago. But this scale is not good. But it's roughly it. You see where I drew it before. Here it looks slightly different, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So let's be precise. This line indicates the positions. Is it of your brigade or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, I will limit myself here to the brigade, to the Kosevo Brigade. So this is the area here. This is the -- to the left is the 1st Romanija and to the right, on the right flank is the Vogosca Brigade, over here, and other brigades in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, are you telling us that on the 12th of December, 1992 where we see this point 6, that the positions changed here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: On the 12th of December, 1992. No, I'm not able to give you a precise answer to that. But at that time they were those shifts, as I have already said. There were those tactical shifts to improve one's positions, and tactical rectification of one's positions doesn't mean advancement only. It also means tactical retreat for about, say, 100 metres, because perhaps then you can take up a better position, better shelters from the fire from the opposite side and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP34, will you please look at another map that you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could both Defence counsel and the witness slow down, because the interpreter is breaking her legs over her own words more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for everything, and I will ask the witness to do that. And I'll do my best to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that I had already slowed down. But it means I have to slow down even further. All right. I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, you have in front of you a map. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: It is the same map except that it is dated 14th of February, 1992, so it is some two months fresher. It's the same map, but the date is two months fresher, newer. It's the same thing. And I shall repeat once again the scale of the map is so unfavourable that one cannot see anything with any accuracy. But that is it. On a map with a larger scale, you can see better, on the first match. But yes, this is -- yes, this is now with corrected lines, with corrected lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but please slow down. Have I understood you correctly? Are you saying that during this period of time this line changed -- this line of your brigade changed to a very insignificant extent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I'm now trying to see how I could answer your question precisely. I said at the beginning that the line remained as such on the whole, but certain trenches would move forward or backwards to the left or the right and this took place in the course of 1993 and 1994 and 1995, on both sides. These actions are customary ones. They are actions that are customary for the company commander who decides about this in the zone of responsibility of his company, and this is the case on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP34, you have another map from this set of three maps in front of you. Could you please put this one here --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I think it's exactly the same as far as the northern battlefield is concerned. Yes, we've already seen that. It's the same again. Let me just see. The 23rd of March, 1993. Again, it shows certain movements at the same place. Yes, at the beginning, as I said, there is a forest here, and this is how you would advance and move backwards. So the front was variable, so to speak. It was alive, in a sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that "it was alive in a sense," that means that in that area there was fighting in the zone of, as you say, one company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The most intense attacks were organised in this area, because the area is such that even a tank can go through it, pass through it, as they say in the army. So there was the danger of tanks penetrating in this part. Do you understand? That's why it's like that. But on the right flank tanks can't pass through the ground, so the way the defence is organised there is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just said that the area where attacks were launched on a daily basis was an area that could be passed through by a tank. With regard to the September 1992-August 1994 period, can you tell us what kind of weapons your brigade had at its disposal. And I'm referring to both light and heavy weapons, if you had any such weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The question is now quite clear to me. I wanted you to be more precise, but it's clear to me now. You said from the beginning up until August 1994. That's the period you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about September 1992-August 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, from February onwards the brigade wasn't in existence any more. The organisation was quite different, but it did have infantry weapons at its disposal. It was organised into battalions and companies, and it had infantry weapons. In addition, it had logistics support. It had artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have any information as to the kind of weapons that the BH army had at its disposal? I'm referring to the units whose positions were facing yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, we did have information, and that could be seen in direct conflicts. On the whole, they had infantry weapons of the same quality, of the same kind. These were weapons used by the former JNA and the former police of Yugoslavia. They had firing weapons, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifle, light machine-guns, et cetera. As far as artillery is concerned, the situation was the same. This is artillery that was used before the conflict broke out, so guns, Howitzers, mortars, tanks, self-propelled weapons, et cetera. It was the same, as far as the quality is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, and I wanted to ask you to speak slowly once more. You have just listed the heavy weapons the enemy had at its disposal. In order to be more precise, could you tell us whether - and I'm referring to the period I have already mentioned, September 1992-February 1994 - as commander of your brigade, did you have any information about the positions of heavy weapons on the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: On the whole, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If the Defence shows you a plan of the -- a map of the town which relates to that area - perhaps it won't cover the whole area, but perhaps it will - could you mark the positions of the heavy weapons that the BH army had as well as your positions, the positions of your heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: If the map is a detailed one, yes, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document is D1836. That is the map of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would it take much time, do you think, this marking, or could it be relatively quickly done? And do you need the markings for your questions to come?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and I don't think this will take very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, can you mark this on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you whether I can mark this with a felt-tip, since Mr. President warned me about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mark it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- With the number "1," for example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Do you mean our positions now, the positions of our artillery, or the positions of the enemy's artillery?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The enemy artillery positions first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The main artillery positions of the enemy side were in the Humsko Brdo, the Humsko hill area. That's here. And I can draw that here. There were mortars here, and then they had something like this and then they had this, like so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, could you move the map a bit to the right and tell us what these symbols indicate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Let's say a mortar then a cannon, a Howitzer, and then they had these mobile -- these mobile guns, tractor -- caterpillar vehicles. They were popularly called "tanks," but they weren't all tanks. That would be it. And one of the directions of action was towards the north, in the direction of the Kosevo Brigade. And here they could cover the west. This is an exceptional site. This is Humsko Brdo, and from here they could fire on the north and the north-west and the west. It's an exceptional position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of the transcript, I don't know how precise I'll be in describing these symbols, but I think it would be sufficient to say that the witness marked a cannon, a mortar -- a mobile mortar --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: No. Not a mobile mortar, a mobile armoured vehicle. That can only be a tank. But in fact it can be both a tank and a self-propelled device.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you say a tank, a self-propelled device --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I was only mentioning one of each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again ask you to slow down. You might not be aware of the speed of your speech, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you marked a cannon, a self-propelled piece, a Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: And a tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And a tank. Can you tell us how many tanks there were, since you say you only made markings for each weapon for one weapon and that you personally know -- do you personally know anything about this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I said where the basic positions were, but there were other positions in enemy territory where the existence of artillery had been recorded. But these were the main positions, and this is where the weapons were most concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Wait for just a moment. Since you said that these were the main firing positions but that there were other firing positions, could you mark the other firing positions on the map, the other ones used by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, a tank was also recorded or self-propelled piece or a tank and a self-propelled piece in the tunnel here. It was observed here for sure. And then in the zone of the school of architecture, action was observed here too, from this area, from this zone. They were either tanks or self-propelled pieces. It wasn't possible to identify this for sure. But there were caterpillar vehicles which moved to one side and to the other side, to the hospital that is up here, the Kosevo hospital. So this is where they would manoeuvre. And the tank was there for a certain period of time and then it left. It was moved, perhaps, to the other side. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, first of all, could you put the numbers "1," "2," and "3," in these circles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, at the positions identified by numbers "1," "2," and "3," the witness indicated that the BH army had its firing positions there. They had heavy weapons there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I haven't finished yet. If I may. You have correctly said that these were heavy weapons, but mobile guns of smaller calibres were a greater problem for us. Eighty-one or 82-millimetre mortars and 60-millimetre mortars which were mounted on mobile vehicles were more serious problems for us. These could be small mobile vehicles or little lorries up to 2 tonnes and they were at various points and it was very difficult to observe these things and to destroy them. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP34, you have now marked these firing positions. Can you now tell us how frequently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, for the transcript, when the witness said "they were at various points," he pointed at the area in the east approximately starting with "3," where it reads "Kosevo hospital," up slowly south to the west covering the whole area where the map reads "Kosevsko Brdo."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, you have marked the firing positions for heavy weapons and you said that the most serious problem was caused by vehicles with mortars. I think you mentioned 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: 82 and 81-millimetre mortars. Both calibres exist, but in fact it's the same kind of mortar. It has the same range and the same performance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, for the period during which you were present up until February 1994, during that period how often did the BH army use these heavy weapons to fire on your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Very often when there was fighting, but there was also sporadic fighting, fighting that would break out suddenly. There would be a lull, it would be calm, and then suddenly a shell would fall, two or three shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have marked the firing positions of the BH army, can you point out to us the location in this zone where the artillery of your brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, you can't see it on this map, but it's to the north, from here to the north. A minute ago I indicated it on the map. It's Pretrzanj. That was our main firing position. But we would move our firing positions too. That was recorded by UNPROFOR, and UNPROFOR observed that. But the main firing position was always on Pretrzanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that this was recorded by UNPROFOR. And given your answer, can you tell us whether there was cooperation on both sides, whether there was mutual cooperation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I suppose it was successful, this cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were the commander of the brigade, did you at any time receive protests according to which artillery was being used from your positions to fire in the direction of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Was I ever warned, did I ever receive a protest?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You personally or someone in your brigade whose responsibility that was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I've understood you. No one in the Kosevo Brigade ever received an official protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "official," I mean written or verbal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. "Official" for me means that someone -- a representative of UNPROFOR comes and protests. But no, that didn't happen. And in written form, no, by no means. We didn't receive any such protests.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have the map in front of us and we can see that it shows the Kosevo hospital area and that we can see the Bare cemetery area on the map as well as the children's hospital area, can you tell us whether at any time during that period while you were the commander did you receive a protest according to which you fired in the direction of the cemetery and the hospital from your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where -- and when I say "where," I mean in what kind of buildings -- was your command post located and the command post of subordinate units if you had any such units during that period and in what buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: In private buildings, the buildings that were there, the command of the brigade was in a private house. It was subsequently in the location of Nahorevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch the first name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I have to be very precise. As I said, the unit consisted of two -- those were divided into two plus three and it had two battalions. That's the form it existed in and operated in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said that "the command of the brigade was in a private house," you then mentioned where it first was. Could you please repeat that name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. But you can't see it on the map. But if it's -- it's the Radava zone, the Radava zone. It's north from here. Radava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the interpreters couldn't hear you. That's reason why I'm asking. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us where the command posts of your brigade and of your subordinate units were located. You say that they were located in private houses. Did you have any information, given that you have told us the 105th Brigade had positions facing yours, towards the south, can you tell us whether you had any information as to the positions of the 105th Brigade. Where were they located, in what kind of buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Information as to the buildings they were in? No, I don't know that for 100 per cent, but I know that they were billeted in private houses just like we were, in private buildings. The buildings that were in their zone of responsibility. Those were the most suitable buildings. They didn't have any traditional barracks, just like -- and similarly we didn't have such barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you were -- what sort of uniforms you wore in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, that's a very interesting question, and that applies to the other side too. At the beginning of the war, if someone had a uniform of the former Yugoslavia, of the former police force, then he would don that uniform. Some people had hunting uniforms. They were camouflage uniforms too, and then they would put those uniforms on. The majority had civilian uniforms, and then gradually the quartermaster supplies increased and we had uniforms, but we never had one single type of uniform right up to the very end of the war, and that applies to us and to the enemy side. That is something that is certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you just speak slowly. Mr. DP34, given that you were the brigade commander, can you tell us whether you as brigade commander issued orders to your subordinates. And if you did, what form did those orders take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes. I issued verbal orders -- written and verbal orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, given the position of the zone of responsibility of your brigade, whether there was an order which was in force while you were the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: What do you mean? I don't understand what you mean when you say "in force." Do you mean whether it was applied, implemented?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I have to say that this brigade - and this is my opinion - was the most disciplined brigade in the corps, and I can claim for certain that all the orders that we received from our superior commanders were implemented and all the orders issued by the command to the subordinate units were implemented. If they weren't, then penalties were imposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were well disciplined and that at times you punished those persons who did not stand by the orders, were there such cases -- what were those transgressions, if I may call them that, which were punished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of such cases. One needs to admit that. There were some disciplinary transgressions, and they ranged from disciplinary transgressions to criminal offences and they were always punished, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But more precise, what were those disciplinary breaches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Disciplinary breaches were the disobeyance of -- disobedience regarding the rule, drunkenness, lack of discipline, brawls and the like, and crimes including murder, so there was also the crime of murder. I think this is the severest crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now I will ask you to explain to us more precisely the murder that you tell us is the severest crime of all. Did it happen in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes, not once but twice during my duty as the commander -- no, sorry, once while I was the commander and the second one happened when I wasn't the commander but it was in that same area. But both times. And later on because that unit remained there and the perpetrators were arrested, the perpetrator was arrested. The court procedure was organised. This was done by the military police. The person was taken under custody to Lukavica, and from what I know after the court procedure he was sentenced to a term of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you told us that you thought that your brigade was well disciplined, that you had it in control. And can you tell us whether in the area of responsibility of your brigade at the time when you commanded that brigade, whether there were some other units - when I say "other units," I mean military units, army units - which were not under your command? And if so, then when were they there and what was your attitude to such units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: First, I want to say that it is not that I think. I affirm -- I put it to you that the troops were very well disciplined. I would say that they were the best disciplined of all. But that does not matter. Your second question: Were there paramilitary units, if I understand your drift. Yes, there were some paramilitary, parapolice units -- well, groups. Yes, there were such cases. And I wish to emphasise that in particular all of this from the territory of the Kosevo Brigade -- that is, this matter was settled, and I think -- no, I do not think. I put it to you that we were the first unit in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and perhaps -- I don't know if we were the only one -- which had resolved this matter once and for all so that, say, sometime as of September 1992 in the area of responsibility -- well, they were never under the command because they were never the proper army but in the area of responsibility of the Kosevo Brigade there wasn't a single paramilitary formation nor a single former paramilitary group as of September 1992. And it took us a great deal of work and effort to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as you were answering this question -- and I think you mentioned that it was the first unit in the Sarajevo Corps which resolved the problem with the para-troops. Do you have any knowledge if in the area of responsibility of other brigades there were also such paramilitary units and whether they constituted such a problem, one of the problems that you as the commander of a brigade solved with other brigade commanders at the level of the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: It was a chronic problem, if I may put it that way. And to my mind, it existed, it survived until the end of the war. It was solved in part but never fully and completely. But the unit which had completely settled the problem of paramilitary units and paramilitary groups, that unit was the Kosevo Brigade. That is what I said. But that problem continued well after that. There were some partial -- but I'm not sure about other units. Of course I'm not referring to all of them I'm not sure that all the units had managed to resolve the problem until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, when you told us that you personally as the commander of -- as the brigade commander carried out all the orders received from your superiors, can you tell us who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The corps commander -- no, sorry, during a period of time -- and there was a rather long period of time when the commander of the tactical group and then the commander -- the corps commander, were my superiors. But the corps commander was my only superior during a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, now that you've answered this question and you said "for a while -- for a period of time the commander of the operative group and target tactical group for a while." Can you be more precise and tell us, between September 1992 until February 1994, were those periods of time when you were under the command of the commander of either the operative group or the tactical group and when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: During that period of time, the Kosevo Brigade was first subordinated to the command of the operative group -- Vogosca operative group. That is what it was called. And it was sometime in the autumn of 1992. I do not remember exactly the date when it ceased to exist. After that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Will you please go slowly. You said the Vogosca operative group. Now, can you be precise and tell us from when until when, that is, when were you under this Vogosca operative group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: It could be in the beginning of May and then until September/October. I really do not remember. But while it was in existence. I think this is precise enough. Until this operative group existed, we were its part. And it is very easy to find the date when it ceased to exist. I simply do not recall it. But as long as it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, during that period of time which units made part of this operative group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The Vogosca operative group incorporated Rajlovac Brigade, the Vogosca Brigade, and Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when you spoke to us about the tactical group -- the Vogosca Tactical Group, can you tell us which period of that time does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, the Vogosca Tactical Group was set up in 1993. And once again, I do not remember the exact date, but I'll be more precise. From its foundation to its disbanding, the Kosevo Brigade was a member of the Vogosca Tactical Group. That is, as of its establishment until it was -- until it stopped existing, we were part of the Vogosca Tactical Group, and its composition was slightly different from that of the Vogosca operative group. It was different because not all the units were in both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You tell us that they did not incorporate identical units, and you gave us the Rajlovac, Vogosca, and Kosevo Brigades. Can you tell us which units were part of the Vogosca Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: The Vogosca Tactical Group, in addition to the above indicated units, that is, the three brigades that were incorporated there, but it also incorporated parts of the Ilidza Brigade, or rather the Ilidza Battalion, part of the Ilijas Brigade, that is the Semizovac Battalion, and some logistic groups, that is, the units were reorganised, reformed, and it was set up different, but it was those units which were already incorporated in this group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP34, now that you've explained to us the structure and the composition of the Vogosca Tactical Group and told us that you were subordinate to the commanders of the operations and subsequently the tactical group, can you also tell us whether you -- did you first -- first, did you report on the situation in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Why, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you put together reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes, reports were written, and they were then submitted to the tactical group, that is, first the commander of the operative group and then to the commander of the tactical group and through them to the corps command. Very important information, we did not have our own codes, so that we had to use the Vogosca Brigade code in the corps command, that is, cables.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how often did you put together these reports and submit them, whether to the commander of the regular or operative group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: We submitted regular reports as requested by the rules and when necessary we also drew up extraordinary reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So now you are telling us that this was one of the manners of reporting in your brigade. You as a brigade commander, whilst you held that post, did you also have briefings in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how often did you have those briefings in the corps command and who attended them. Would you be present alone, or would they be broader meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, your question is pretty broad, but I'll try to be precise once again. So yes, I attended those briefings. They were relatively frequent, that is, all the briefings that were organised by the corps. So not in the corps command but organised by the corps command, and it could take place elsewhere, not necessarily on the corps premises. And this happened once or twice a month. And those briefings were attended by members of the corps command. As a rule, the commander or the chief of staff of the corps then whilst there were the operative or tactical group, the commanders of the tactical, that is, operative group, brigade commanders. Then, at times, representatives of civilians, of civilian organisations, representatives of the police, and that would be it. But that was only now and then, I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the corps commander attend those briefings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: I've said it already. Yes, he was present there. If not, then such meetings were chaired by the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, at those briefings at which you were present, which subjects did you broach? What were the contents of those briefings in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34
utterances.text: Well, what else could it be but -- we called them "reporting." That is, we submitted our reports there, the subordinate commanders in the area of responsibility of the corps submitted their reports. So then we would analyse the previous period and be issued -- and be assigned tasks for the forthcoming period, that is, we would discuss problems in the army and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are close to the time where we have to adjourn. And if this would be a suitable moment, then we'll adjourn now. Mr. DP34, I have to ask you to come back next Monday. We'll not sit in the morning but we'll sit in the afternoon. That means that we -- that we will sit on from 2.15 p.m. in another courtroom, Courtroom I. I'd like to instruct you not to speak to anyone about the testimony you have given or the testimony you are still about to give, not with anyone, not with the Defence, not with the Prosecution, not with Judges if you would see them during the weekend. So this is my instruction. I wish everyone as good a weekend as can be, and we'll adjourn until quarter past 2.00 next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry. If you will excuse me. Just one thing that I need to point out. In the French transcript, on page 77, lines 11 and 12 were not translated. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid I can't do it now right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 77, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 77, a few lines are not translated. I take it that proper care will be taken when -- even if we are not working, other people are working on the transcript. We'll adjourn until next Monday.
